chapter_title: Introduction to Scripting with C# in Unity

screens.title: Introduction to Scripting with C# in Unity
screens.subtitle: Attach logic to GameObjects so they move, react, and behave

narration.text: Scripting is what turns a static scene into an interactive experience. In Unity, we write behavior in C-sharp, create scripts that act as components, and attach them to GameObjects to give them logic. In this lesson you’ll learn how to create a script asset, why your class must inherit from the engine’s base behavior, and how simple lifecycle methods let you initialize and update behavior continuously. You will also learn practical debugging: printing log messages and checking the Console, and an essential performance habit — making movement frame-rate independent by using the frame time value. The concrete skill here is to create a script, attach it to a cube, make the cube rotate reliably, and observe log output to confirm the script runs. This matters because nearly every interactive mechanic in your game — movement, input handling, state changes — is implemented through scripts. As you work, watch for common beginner mistakes: mismatched file and class names, unsaved edits, or forgetting to use the frame delta when you move objects. By the end you’ll know how to wire code to objects and verify behavior using the Console. Ready to build your first Rotator?

keyIdea.title: Script = Component + Logic
keyIdea.text: A C# script in Unity is a Component you attach to a GameObject to define interactive behavior and lifecycle callbacks.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of these lessons you will understand how C-sharp scripts add behavior to GameObjects, create and attach a basic script, and use the most important lifecycle methods correctly. First, you will be able to explain the role of a script as a component and why inheriting from the engine base class matters. Second, you will create a new C-sharp file and ensure the class name and file name match so Unity can compile and attach the script without errors. Third, you will write and run simple code that logs messages and alters a GameObject’s transform to create motion. Finally, you will consistently use the frame-time value to make movement frame-rate independent and debug issues using the Console. Each objective is taught with a concrete example: rotating a Cube, printing a startup message, and adjusting a public speed value in the Inspector. Along the way we'll discuss common mistakes like unsaved scripts, missing component references, and forgetting to multiply by the frame delta. These objectives are practical; they map directly onto actions you will take in the Editor and the Console, and mastering them sets a foundation for larger gameplay systems. Are you ready to practice these skills?

screens.title: How these skills map to practice
screens.subtitle: Actionable outcomes and quick checks

narration.text: These objectives are intentionally practical so you can measure progress immediately in the Editor. When you create a new C-sharp file named Rotator and implement a public speed variable, you should be able to attach that file to a Cube and change the speed value in the Inspector to see the effect in Play mode. When you place a Debug print in Start, a single message should appear in the Console when you press Play, confirming the script ran. When you move code into Update for continuous motion, you should see smooth rotation if you use the frame-time value; if rotation jumps or scales with frame-rate, that signals a missing delta-time multiplication. A useful habit is to save the script, return to Unity, and watch the Console for compile errors before pressing Play. These checks map directly to the four objective cards: role of script, create and attach, lifecycle methods, and debugging with frame independence. Practically, practice these checks now: create the file, match class and file names, attach, save, press Play, and observe the Console. Each step reinforces the mapping between code and behavior.

screens.title: What a C# script is in Unity
screens.subtitle: Scripts are components that define behavior and access engine features

narration.text: A C-sharp script in Unity is not just a text file; it becomes a Component when you attach it to a GameObject. In practical terms, that means the script holds logic and data that act on the GameObject through the engine. The script file contains a public class that, when it inherits from the engine’s base component class, gains engine callbacks and shortcuts like the transform property. For example, a script named CubeRotator with a public class of the same name can rotate its GameObject by calling rotation functions on transform. A common misconception is to treat script files like standalone programs. In Unity, scripts run inside the engine context and are driven by lifecycle callbacks rather than starting at a main function. Another mistake is renaming the file but not the class; that breaks the attachment and causes compilation confusion. A concrete scenario: you create Rotator. cs, define a public float speed, attach the script to a cube, and then adjust speed in the Inspector to see immediate changes during Play mode. The key takeaway is that scripts are reusable, attachable components that operate on GameObjects through engine-provided hooks. How might you design a script so it can be reused across multiple GameObjects with different settings?

keyIdea.title: Script = Attach + Behavior
keyIdea.text: When a script inherits from the engine base, it becomes a Component attached to a GameObject and gains lifecycle methods and shortcuts.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › What a C# script is
Definition

Script as a Component

A C# file with a public class that inherits from the engine base becomes a Component that can be attached to GameObjects to add logic and state.

  • Gains lifecycle callbacks like Start and Update.
  • Has automatic access to the GameObject's Transform via a transform shortcut.
  • Exposes public fields to the Inspector for quick tuning.
Analogy
Think of a script like a behavior module you plug into a toy: the module defines what the toy can do, and you can swap modules to change behavior while keeping the same body.
Example
Rotator.cs with a public speed value rotates a cube when attached and run in Play mode. Adjusting speed in the Inspector changes rotation immediately.
Common Mistake
Renaming the file without renaming the public class breaks Unity's expectation and can prevent the script from compiling or attaching properly. Always keep file and class names matched.
Pro Tip
Use meaningful names like PlayerMovement or CubeRotator so the purpose is clear when you attach the component.
Key Takeaway

Scripts are attachable components; inheritance grants access to engine hooks and shorthand properties like transform.

screens.title: Create a C# script asset and open it
screens.subtitle: From Project folder to code editor in a few steps

narration.text: Creating a script in Unity is a simple but repeatable process that connects the Editor and your code editor. Start by making a folder named _Scripts in the Project window to keep code organized. Right-click the folder and choose to create a C-sharp Script, then give it a clear name such as Rotator. The important rule is to make the class name inside the script match the file name; if you rename the file later, also rename the class to avoid compile errors. Double-clicking the asset opens your configured code editor where you'll see a small template: a using statement for the engine, a public class inheriting from the engine base, and placeholder methods for Start and Update. This template shows how the engine expects your code to be structured and provides a safe place to add initialization and per-frame logic. A common beginner pitfall is editing the wrong file or forgetting to save before switching back to the Editor; unsaved changes won't compile. Another is importing code with syntax errors that prevent the Editor from entering Play mode. Practically, create the script, open it, add a Debug print in Start, save, return to Unity, and verify the Console shows the message when you press Play. How will you name your next script to make its role obvious?

keyIdea.title: File → Class match
keyIdea.text: Name a C# file to match its public class and save before returning to the Editor to ensure successful compilation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Create & Open Script
Steps
  1. Create a _Scripts folder in the Project window to stay organized.
  2. Right-click > Create > C# Script and name it descriptively (e.g., Rotator).
  3. Double-click the asset to open it in your code editor and inspect the MonoBehaviour template.
  4. Make sure the public class name matches the file name and save changes before returning to Unity.
This process ensures your asset compiles and appears as a Component you can attach immediately. If the Console shows compile errors, it typically points to a naming or syntax issue that needs fixing in the editor.
Code Template (visual)
using UnityEngine;

public class Rotator : MonoBehaviour
{
    void Start()
    {
        Debug.Log("Rotator started on: " + gameObject.name);
    }

    void Update()
    {
        // per-frame logic goes here
    }
}
Save after editing so Unity compiles the latest version.
Common Pitfall
Renaming the file without renaming the public class causes compile errors and prevents attachment.

screens.title: MonoBehaviour and why to inherit from it
screens.subtitle: Gain lifecycle methods and engine integration

narration.text: MonoBehaviour is the base class provided by the engine that gives scripts the ability to attach to GameObjects and receive callbacks at specific points of their lifetime. When your public class inherits from MonoBehaviour, Unity can treat instances of that class as Components and call methods such as Start and Update at the right times. Without that inheritance your class is a plain C-sharp type; it can still contain logic and be used as a helper or data container, but it cannot be attached to a GameObject or receive engine callbacks automatically. A concrete example: by inheriting, you can place a Debug print in Start to confirm the script enabled at runtime and put movement code in Update to execute every frame. A common misconception is that inheritance is optional for everything; it is optional if you intend to use the class as a pure utility, but mandatory if you want the engine to manage the instance as a Component. Knowing this distinction helps you design clean code: keep engine-dependent behavior in MonoBehaviour scripts and reusable logic in plain classes that MonoBehaviour scripts can invoke. Consider the design choice: when should a helper class be plain and when should it inherit and be attached?

keyIdea.title: Inheritance enables integration
keyIdea.text: If you want Unity to manage a script as a Component with callbacks, inherit from the engine base; otherwise use plain classes for pure logic.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › MonoBehaviour
Claim

Inherit to get engine callbacks

MonoBehaviour makes your class attachable and driven by the engine lifecycle methods like Start and Update. It also provides convenience properties like transform and gameObject.

  • Start runs once when enabled.
  • Update runs each frame while enabled.
  • Access helpful properties without extra lookups.
Design Note
Keep engine interaction in MonoBehaviour scripts and move pure logic to plain classes. This keeps components simple and reusable.
Example
A movement controller class could use a helper pathfinding class that does not inherit. The controller stays attached to a GameObject while the helper remains a plain C# class invoked by it.
A misconception to avoid: inheriting from the base just to access utility functions. Instead, prefer composition and call plain classes from your MonoBehaviour when appropriate.
Common Mistake
Making all classes inherit from the engine base bloats components and tightly couples non-UI logic to the engine lifecycle.

screens.title: Start() — one-time initialization
screens.subtitle: Use Start to set up references, initial values, and print startup logs

narration.text: Start is called once for a script instance, just before the first frame when the script becomes enabled. Use Start for one-time setup tasks: caching component references, initializing variables, subscribing to events, or printing a confirmation to the Console. For example, placing a log statement in Start that prints the GameObject's name confirms the script executed at startup and helps track which instance ran. A common mistake is to place expensive or repeated work in Start that actually belongs in a different stage, or to assume Start runs in construction order for multiple objects — initialization ordering can vary. Another frequent confusion is using Start for physics initialization that should instead be placed in the fixed-timestep callback; physics setup often belongs in the fixed-update flow. When you add a Debug message in Start and press Play, you should see exactly one message per active instance, which is a quick sanity check that your component enabled correctly. Key practice: use Start for initialization only, keep it fast, and rely on Update or other callbacks for ongoing behavior. Think about what needs to happen once versus every frame when you design your component.

keyIdea.title: Use Start for init
keyIdea.text: Start runs once and is the right place for quick setup, references, and a single confirmation log to the Console.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Start Method
When to use Start
One-time initialization tasks that should run when the component first becomes enabled.
  • Cache references like GetComponent calls.
  • Initialize default values and public fields if needed.
  • Log a startup message to verify the component enabled.
Example
Debug.Log("Rotator started on: " + gameObject.name) will print one line per active Rotator when Play begins, confirming correct attachment.
Misconception
Start is not a constructor. Avoid heavy synchronous work here that could stall loading; prefer short initializations or deferred loading strategies.
If you need physics setup that depends on the physics engine's fixed update timing, consider a fixed-timestep callback instead of Start.
Key Takeaway
Keep Start concise: set up references, default values, and a single log for verification.

screens.title: Update() — continuous per-frame behavior
screens.subtitle: Put movement, input checks, and per-frame calculations here

narration.text: Update is the heartbeat of many gameplay scripts: it runs once every frame while the script is enabled. Use Update for tasks that must be checked or applied repeatedly, like polling player input, animating transforms, or running time-based calculations. Because Update runs so often, efficiency matters: avoid expensive allocations, heavy loops, or redundant component lookups inside Update. A concrete example is rotating an object: using a rotate call multiplied by a speed value and the frame-time variable produces smooth, consistent rotation. An important misconception to correct is thinking Update provides a fixed time step; it does not. Frame durations vary, so you must scale movement with the frame-time value to achieve consistent per-second motion. Another common mistake is doing physics force applications in Update instead of the fixed-timestep callback designed for physics calculations. When you place logic in Update, test under different simulated frame rates or use toggles that reduce performance to ensure behavior remains stable. The closing question: when you need smooth movement and consistent results, how will you structure Update to minimize allocations and use the frame-time value safely?

keyIdea.title: Update is per-frame
keyIdea.text: Use Update for repeated checks and movement, and scale by the frame-time value to keep behavior consistent across varying frame rates.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Update Method
What Update does
Update executes once per frame and is suited for continuous behaviors like input checks and transform changes.
  • Handle input polling and timers.
  • Apply object motion and rotations.
  • Avoid allocations and repeated lookups inside Update for performance.
Example
Applying rotation each frame with a speed multiplied by the frame-time value produces frame-rate independent motion and smooth animation.
Misconception
Update is not fixed-rate. Using it for physics that require a fixed timestep can cause jitter. Use the engine's fixed-timestep callback for physics operations.
To improve performance, cache references in Start and avoid allocating memory inside Update, such as string concatenations or new object creation on every frame.
Key Takeaway
Keep Update lean, scale by frame time, and reserve heavy work for less frequent callbacks.

screens.title: Debug.Log and the Console
screens.subtitle: Print messages to verify script execution and variable values

narration.text: Debug printing is one of the fastest ways to verify that your code runs and to inspect variables during development. The engine provides a print function that sends messages to the Console window. Place a message in Start to confirm that a component enabled once, or print variable values in Update to watch changes over time. For example, printing the GameObject's name in Start lets you confirm which object the script attached to. A useful trick is to include context in the message so Console lines are easy to filter: include the component name and a short value. Beginners often forget that the Console can filter messages by type or hide logs, so if your message doesn't appear check the Console filters. Another common oversight is leaving verbose logs in Update during performance tests; heavy logging every frame can slow your test and clutter the Console. Always remove or gate high-frequency logs before profiling or releasing. Try this exercise: add a print in Start that includes the object name, save, return to the Editor, press Play, and confirm a single log line appears. What meaningful context will you include in your next debug message?

keyIdea.title: Use the Console early
keyIdea.text: Logging confirms execution and helps inspect values; include context and avoid high-frequency logs during performance tests.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Debug.Log & Console
Why Log
Quickly verify that a script ran and inspect runtime values without attaching a debugger.
// Example message in Start
Debug.Log("Rotator started on: " + gameObject.name);
Include the component name and a short label so messages are useful when multiple objects log similar lines.
Console Tips
  • Check Console filters if you don’t see messages.
  • Avoid logging every frame during profiling; it can affect performance.
  • Use logs for quick checks and a debugger for complex state introspection.
Key Takeaway

Use informative Console messages for startup verification, then remove or reduce frequency before performance tests.

screens.title: Using transform and Time.deltaTime
screens.subtitle: Make movement consistent by scaling by the frame-time value

narration.text: The transform property is a convenient shortcut available to scripts inheriting from the engine base; it gives immediate access to a GameObject’s position, rotation, and scale. When you move or rotate objects in Update, you must scale your motion by the frame-time value so the action happens per second rather than per frame. For example, rotating along the Y axis by multiplying a speed value by the frame time produces consistent rotation regardless of the current frame rate. A common beginner error is to omit the frame-time multiplication and watch movement speed vary on different machines or under load. Another practical point: use the engine's rotate or translate functions on transform to apply relative motion, and avoid directly setting position when smoother interpolation is needed. A concrete walkthrough: add transform. Rotate(0, speed * Time. deltaTime, 0) inside Update, set speed to a public float, save, attach the script, press Play, and then change speed in the Inspector to observe the effect. The closing question: how will you test that motion remains steady when the frame rate drops? Using transform and Time.deltaTime means multiply movement by time.deltatime so position and rotation happen consistently per second, not per frame.. In practical terms, make movement consistent by scaling by the frame-time value. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Frame-rate independence
keyIdea.text: Multiply movement by Time.deltaTime so position and rotation happen consistently per second, not per frame.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › transform & Time.deltaTime
Concept
transform provides direct control over an object’s position and rotation. Time.deltaTime represents the seconds since the last frame.
// Rotate Y-axis at 'speed' degrees per second
transform.Rotate(0, speed * Time.deltaTime, 0);
Example
Set public float speed to 50. In Play mode the cube should rotate smoothly at 50 degrees per second, even if fps changes.
Misconception
Applying motion without the frame-time value causes speed to scale with frame rate. Test under different frame rates to confirm stability.
Pro tip: expose speed as a public field so you can tune it in the Inspector at runtime for quick iteration.
Key Takeaway
Always scale per-frame motion by the frame-time value to ensure consistent behavior across devices.

screens.title: Hands-on: make a Cube rotate and log a message
screens.subtitle: Create a Rotator script, attach it, and verify in the Console

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through the exact steps to make a Cube rotate and print a startup message. First, create a new Scene and save it with a clear name. In the Project window make a _Scripts folder and create a C-sharp Script called Rotator. Open the script and add a public float rotationSpeed and a Debug print in Start that includes the GameObject name. Then implement rotation inside Update using the frame-time value. Save the file, return to the Editor, create a 3D Cube, and drag the Rotator script onto it. Select the Cube and in the Inspector set a rotation speed value. Press Play: you should see the cube rotate and a single Console message confirming the script started on that cube. If the cube does not rotate, check the Console for compile errors and make sure the script is saved and attached. A frequent beginner error is changing values in Play mode and expecting them to persist; remember Inspector changes during Play are temporary. This exercise reinforces the loop: edit, save, attach, play, and inspect. How will you vary rotationSpeed to test behavior?

keyIdea.title: Practice loop
keyIdea.text: Edit script, save, attach to GameObject, press Play, inspect the Console and Inspector to confirm behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Hands-on Activity
Activity Steps
  1. Create and save a new Scene named ScriptingScene.
  2. Create a Cube in the Hierarchy.
  3. Create a _Scripts folder and add Rotator.cs.
  4. Edit Rotator: add public float rotationSpeed, Debug.Log in Start, and rotate using rotationSpeed * Time.deltaTime in Update.
  5. Save, attach Rotator to the Cube, set rotationSpeed, press Play, and check the Console for the startup log.
Expected Result
The cube rotates continuously and the Console shows one startup message naming the Cube. Tweak rotationSpeed in the Inspector during Play to see immediate effect.
Common Mistakes
  • Forgetting to save the script before returning to the Editor.
  • Renaming file without renaming the class.
  • Not attaching the script to the Cube in the Hierarchy.
Pro Tip
Use Console filters and pausing to capture and inspect startup logs if too many messages appear during tests.

screens.title: Common beginner mistakes and how to fix them
screens.subtitle: Naming, unsaved files, missing attachments, and frame-time errors

narration.text: When learning scripting in the engine, several recurring mistakes slow down trainees. First, renaming the file but not the public class leads to compilation errors or scripts that don't attach; the fix is to keep the file and class names synchronized. Second, forgetting to save your edits before returning to the Editor means Unity compiles an older version and behavior appears unchanged; always save before switching back. Third, not attaching the script to the intended GameObject is a simple oversight; verifying the component appears in the Inspector solves it. Fourth, forgetting to multiply motion by the frame-time value causes movement to vary with frame-rate; multiply speed by the frame delta to make motion per second consistent. Another common error is placing heavy computation in Update, which can cause performance spikes; instead cache references in Start and minimize allocations in Update. A practical debugging routine is: save, check Console for compile errors, verify the script is attached in the Inspector, press Play, and watch for expected Console messages. These fixes will speed up your iteration loop and reduce time spent diagnosing simple errors. Which of these checks will you add to your pre-Play checklist?

keyIdea.title: Pre-Play Checklist
keyIdea.text: Save scripts, check Console for compile errors, confirm attachment in Inspector, and scale motion by frame-time before pressing Play.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Common Mistakes
Mistake vs Fix
Mismatched File/Class
Rename the public class to match the file or rename the file to match the class.
Unsaved Changes
Save the script before switching to the Editor; unsaved edits are not compiled.
No Attachment
Drag the script onto the GameObject and confirm it appears in the Inspector.
Missing frame-time
Multiply movement or rotation by the frame-time value for consistent speed across devices.
Pre-Play Checklist
  1. Save your script in the editor.
  2. Check the Console for compile errors and address them.
  3. Confirm the script appears in the GameObject's Inspector.
  4. Press Play and confirm expected Console messages and movement behavior.
Pro Tip
Use descriptive log messages and reduce logging frequency during performance tests to keep the Console useful.

screens.title: Expose variables to the Inspector for rapid tuning
screens.subtitle: Use public fields to tune behavior without code edits

narration.text: One of Unity's most useful iteration features is the Inspector, which exposes public fields on a Component for editing in the Editor. By declaring a public float rotationSpeed, or by marking a private field with an expose attribute, you can adjust behavior at runtime without changing code and recompiling. This is invaluable when tuning gameplay: change the speed slider while the game runs, observe the result instantly, and then copy the tuned value back into your script if you want it to persist. Beginners sometimes expect these changes to survive Play mode; remember Inspector edits made during Play are temporary unless applied before exiting Play. Another design consideration is to prefer public fields for tuning values but keep complex state private to avoid accidental external modification. A concrete pattern: expose tuning variables such as speed or acceleration, cache component references in Start, and compute per-frame changes in Update. This separation makes scripts both easy to tune and safe to use across multiple GameObjects with different parameter values. When will you expose a value to the Inspector versus keeping it hard-coded?

keyIdea.title: Tune in Inspector
keyIdea.text: Expose public fields for quick runtime tuning; remember Play-mode changes are temporary and keep sensitive state private.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Inspector Tuning
Pattern
Declare public fields for tunable parameters like rotationSpeed. Use private fields for internal state.
public float rotationSpeed = 50f; // editable in Inspector
Example workflow
Tune rotationSpeed while in Play to find a satisfying value, then copy it back into the script if you want to persist it outside Play mode.
Misconception
Don't assume Inspector edits during Play persist. They are temporary unless explicitly applied after exiting Play mode.
Design tip: prefer explanatory default values and clear field names so teammates can tune behavior without reading code.
Key Takeaway
Expose tuning parameters for rapid iteration and keep core state private to avoid accidental changes.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Keep these core ideas close as you build: scripts are Components that become part of GameObjects when they inherit from the engine base; Start is for one-time initialization; Update runs per frame and must be efficient; Debug prints and the Console are your fastest verification tools; and always scale motion by the frame-time value to ensure consistent behavior across different frame rates. Practically, follow a short loop when things don’t work: save your script, check the Console for compile errors, ensure the script is attached in the Inspector, press Play, and verify output. Expose tuning parameters in the Inspector for rapid iteration, but remember Play-mode edits are temporary. If you adopt these habits early, you’ll iterate faster and avoid common beginner pitfalls, making it easier to implement and test gameplay mechanics reliably. Which single habit from this list will you adopt first to make your debugging loop faster?

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Scripts run inside the engine as Components; use lifecycle methods appropriately and validate behavior with the Console and Inspector.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Key Concepts
C# Scripts
Scripts act as Components that attach to GameObjects and hold behavior.
Lifecycle
Start for setup, Update for per-frame logic; choose the right callback for the job.
Frame Independence
Multiply motion by the frame-time value to keep speed consistent across devices.
Summary
Scripts + lifecycle methods + Console checks = reliable iteration. Keep code organized and use the Inspector to tune values quickly.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three short reminders to keep you productive

narration.text: Keep these three short reminders at hand as you script: match file and class names to avoid compile issues; use Start for one-time setup and Update for repeated logic while scaling motion by the frame-time value; and use Debug logs plus the Console to validate behavior quickly. Practically, run a short pre-Play checklist: save your edits, check for compile errors, confirm attachment in the Inspector, and press Play to see expected Console output. These habits shorten the feedback loop and let you experiment faster with gameplay parameters. Which reminder will you pin to your editor as you practice? Key Concepts — Quick Reference means match names, choose lifecycle methods deliberately, and verify with console messages.. In practical terms, three short reminders to keep you productive. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Match names, choose lifecycle methods deliberately, and verify with Console messages.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Quick Reference
01 — Naming
File name and public class name must match to compile and attach cleanly.
02 — Lifecycle
Start is for initialization; Update is for per-frame behavior; pick appropriately.
03 — Frame Time
Multiply movement by the frame-time value to ensure consistent speed across systems.
Takeaway
Adopt a quick save, check, attach, play loop and use Inspector tuning for rapid iteration.
